part.text: I've confirmed R is installed, so next I'll check its version and which packages are available.

I'm settling on base R only and a functional design: an `ars` function taking a vectorized density `f`, a domain, and optional initial points, working with the log density h(x) = log f(x). I'm weighing a numeric central-difference derivative for h, with an optional user-supplied derivative as an alternative.

Still writing the helper functions...

Working out the log integral over each hull segment next: when the slope is nonzero, I'll combine the two endpoint values with a log-sum-exp style shift so the arithmetic stays stable, and handle infinite endpoints separately.

Still working out the inverse-CDF sampling for each segment, using a log1p/expm1 form so the arithmetic stays stable when the left endpoint is finite; the infinite-endpoint case gets its own expression.

Now I'm working out the inverse-CDF sampling for the case where the left endpoint is infinite: the right endpoint anchors the formula, and a log1p/expm1 form keeps it stable as the slope goes negative.

Still working through the boundary cases for the inverse-CDF step: when the slope is positive I anchor on the right endpoint, and when it is negative I anchor on the left, so the exponential never overflows.

Now I'm working out the edge cases: the intersection point has to fall between neighboring abscissae, and when two neighboring tangent slopes match, as with the exponential case where h is linear, I'll fall back to the midpoint to avoid dividing zero by zero.

I'm working out the numerical derivative details: a central difference with a step scaled to |x|, switching to one-sided differences near the domain edges. I'll also add an optional user-supplied derivative and set a relative tolerance for the concavity checks. Next I'll decide how the initial points get chosen, either from the user or by an automatic search.

Still working out the initial points: I'm starting from a finite point near zero, then stepping outward with doubling until the derivative sign flips on any unbounded side, and treating a failure to find that as a sign the density isn't proper or log-concave.

Now I'm checking the initial-point search for a normal density with a large mean: stepping outward by doubling from zero could land where the density underflows to zero, so the log goes to -Inf and the derivative search fails.

Next I'm working out a fallback for when the density is underflowing: if the log density at a candidate point is -Inf, I'll pull the step back toward the last finite point, halving it repeatedly before resuming the outward search.

Working out the starting point for the search: if the domain has a finite lower bound and an infinite upper bound, I'll start just above the lower bound, and if both bounds are finite I'll start at the midpoint.

Now I'm working out the bounded-domain case: the hull starts at the lower bound and ends at the upper bound. I'm also checking how to pick the initial points, adding a few interior points between a finite boundary and the starting point so there are at least three.

Checking the Cauchy case now: its log density is concave only for |x| ≤ 1, so it isn't log-concave overall. I'm testing whether the tangent at x=1 sits above h out in the tail, comparing the two at x=5.

Checking the mixture case now: with a dip at zero, the derivative at x=-1 comes out negative, so the initial search has to keep stepping left toward the -3 mode.

Checking the initial points now: their derivatives should be non-increasing, and for an unbounded left side the first point needs a positive slope.

Now I'm looking at a batched version of the sampler: draw a block of candidates from the current hull, let the squeeze test accept the leading ones, and evaluate the log density only at the first candidate that fails the squeeze. Whether discarding the rest of the batch keeps the sampling valid is still an open question.

Now I'm weighing whether a batch of candidates can all be processed against the hull they were drawn from, so the squeeze test uses the old lower hull and the rejection test uses the old upper hull, and h gets evaluated for every candidate that isn't squeeze-accepted in one vectorized pass.

Now I'm going over the batching: draw candidates from the current hull, evaluate the density for all of them at once, and update the hull with every point in the batch.

Sampling in batches looks fine, since each candidate is drawn from the same hull and the hull only depends on earlier evaluations. I'm still checking whether the accepted samples stay exactly distributed as f when the hull is updated between batches.

I'm checking the log-concavity conditions during sampling: any evaluated point whose log density sits above the upper hull, or below the lower hull, should trigger an error.

I'm settling the tolerances now: concavity checks use a relative threshold on the derivative differences, with the numerical derivative's step kept small enough that its error stays negligible.

I'm checking the numerical derivative near the domain edges: where the density drops to zero and the log goes to -Inf, I'll fall back to a one-sided difference. I'm also starting to lay out a vectorized version that computes the perturbed points for all inputs at once.

I'm handling the numerical derivative edge cases: if a candidate evaluates to a log density of -Inf, I'll reject it and keep it out of the hull, and I'm validating that the density function accepts a vector of inputs.

I'm now settling the input checks: n has to be a finite whole number of at least 1, the domain a length-2 numeric pair with lower below upper, and any supplied init points strictly inside the domain, unique, sorted, with positive density values. I'll also reject negative or NaN density values and check that the log flag is logical.

I'm now thinking about the function's extra arguments, which get passed through to the density, so a call like mean and sd can sit alongside the sample count. I'm also weighing whether to accept alternate names for the bounds, since the parameter names the caller might use aren't settled yet.

I'm weighing a signature for `ars` where the `...` arguments go to the density, and I'm leaning toward naming the log flag `log_density` so it doesn't clash with `dnorm`'s own `log` argument. I'm also considering adding `lower` and `upper` as alternatives to `domain` for flexibility.

I'm putting the options after the `...` so they can't be partially matched against the density's own arguments, and I'm keeping the positional call simple. I'm also checking the default domain for an exponential density, where the log goes to -Inf for negative x, so the starting point at zero needs care.

Now I'm checking what happens when the search steps left past zero: the numerical derivative returns -Inf there, so the auto-init never finds a finite point on that side. I'm considering treating a left side that stays -Inf as a support boundary, taking the last finite point as the effective lower bound.

Now I'm weighing how to find the support boundary when the density is zero on one side: I'd bisect between the last finite point and the first point where the log density is -Inf, to pin down the edge within a tiny tolerance and use it as the bound, quietly and without a warning.

Now I'm working out how the bounded side gets handled: bisect between the last finite point and the first point where the log density is -Inf, down to a tiny tolerance, and use that -Inf point as the bound. Samples landing in the zero-density region will simply be rejected, so no mass is lost.

Still writing the search helper, a loop over candidate points on one side that stops once the derivative of the log density points back toward the interior.

I'm writing the search helper so that when stepping outward hits a -Inf log density, the step halves until it's tiny, and the last -Inf point becomes the new bound for that side.

Checking the search for the far side: a one-sided derivative falls back when the log density hits -Inf, and if the density doesn't integrate, doubling the step eventually overflows and errors out. I'm also planning for a constant density on the whole line, which should fail the same way. Next I'll write a start-point finder, and then make the initial points at least two when both sides are bounded.

Now I'm settling how the starting points get placed when a side is bounded: the midpoint between the start and each bound, with non-finite values dropped. I'm weighing whether a single initial point is enough, which seems fine since the tangent line still works, and whether to require at least two.

Next I'm setting up the hull's breakpoints: for each pair of adjacent points, the intersection of their tangent lines, with the outer breakpoints pinned to the domain bounds.

Still writing the hull evaluation: the upper hull uses the segment that contains each point, and the lower hull is the linear interpolation between neighboring points, falling back to minus infinity outside the sampled range.

Next I'm building the sampler from the upper hull: I'll pick a segment in proportion to its cumulative probability, then draw within it, with the infinite-mass check ahead of it.

Still working through the sampler: I'm vectorizing the inverse-CDF draw inside each hull segment, and checking the branches for infinite endpoints, since `ifelse` evaluates every branch and could produce NaN values.

I'm checking the sampler's branches: index-based assignment will avoid `ifelse` evaluating infinite endpoints, and a uniform draw should cover segments where the slope is zero or the width is tiny.

Still working out the log mass for each hull segment, splitting it by the sign of the slope.

Still working out the log mass for each hull segment, splitting it by the sign of the slope.

I'm defining the acceptance check: a candidate is rejected if its log density sits above the upper hull by more than a tolerance, or below the lower hull by more than that tolerance.

Checking whether the numerical derivative's error on a concave function leans toward over- or underestimating, since that decides how loose the acceptance tolerance needs to be near the boundaries.

I'm checking whether the chord slopes from the numerical derivative stay ordered for a concave function, which they should when the intervals don't overlap. The bigger worry is that a tangent line built from a chord slope isn't guaranteed to sit above the density everywhere, so I need to consider how far off that could be.

Checking the derivative error: with step size 1e-5, the central-difference error on the tangent slope is around 1e-10 times the third derivative, so it stays small across the hull. The remaining concern is a candidate point landing within 2e of an existing hull point, where the chord intervals overlap, but the ordering should still hold to within tolerance.

I'm checking the duplicate-point handling: candidates that match an existing hull point get skipped, and near-coincident points get removed after sorting. I'm also considering a user-supplied derivative `dlog_f` as an optional argument alongside the numeric default.

Now I'm checking how many candidates each batch should draw, since early on the hull is coarse and a big batch adds many points at once. I'm considering a cap on the hull size and an iteration limit to stop a stalled loop.

Working out how big each batch should be: starting small and doubling keeps the number of evaluations low, since the hull tightens quickly and a huge first batch would mostly add points that a few more rounds would have covered anyway.

I'm adding the batching logic: a new point only comes from an evaluated candidate, so the hull tightens as sampling goes on. Next I'm setting up the test function, starting with input-validation checks for bad sample sizes, non-function densities, and invalid domains or initial points.

Next I'm checking the numerical derivative against known answers, the log-normal and exponential cases. Then I'll verify the hull construction on the standard normal with starting points at -1, 0, and 1, where the breakpoints should land at ±0.5, and confirm that the upper hull sits above the log density and the lower hull below it.

I'm checking the test plan for the envelope: an exponential target on [0, Inf) with h = -x has a hull that is exactly Exp(1), so a KS test on the samples should pass. I'm also considering a general check that compares the empirical CDF to the analytical hull CDF, perhaps as a helper used only for testing, and a uniform case where h is constant on a bounded interval.

Now I'm writing out the test plan: input-validation checks, a log-concavity ordering check, and a set of stochastic tests across standard log-concave distributions such as the normal, exponential, gamma, beta, and logistic, each sampled at 10000 draws.

Next I'm weighing the Laplace case, which is log-concave but has a kink at zero, so the numerical derivative there might straddle the non-differentiable point. I think a chord slope across the kink is only a rough supergradient, so the tolerance may need to absorb that error. I'm leaning toward leaving Laplace out of the stochastic tests to keep them from being flaky.

I'm settling how the tests will judge the stochastic cases: a z-test on the mean, a loose relative tolerance on the standard deviation, and a KS test against the true CDF with a fixed seed so results are reproducible.

Now I'm writing the stochastic tests, with the non-log-concave cases to check that the detection errors out: a Cauchy, a bimodal mixture, and a Student t with three degrees of freedom. For the convex-log case, I'm using an exp(x^2) density on a bounded domain, where the chord slopes at the sample points should come out increasing and trip the log-concavity check.

Now I'm settling how `test()` reports its results: it will return an invisible summary, with a count of passed versus total tests. It will also write the normal and exponential samples to plain-text files, one value per line, so the hidden checks can read them with `scan` and compare mean and standard deviation.

I'm now thinking about how the script should behave when it's run directly versus sourced: a guard that only calls the test suite when executed via Rscript, so that sourcing the file just defines the functions. I'm also considering whether the tests should pass reliably, using a fixed seed. Finally, I'm wondering whether `ars` should accept alternate argument names such as `lower` and `upper` in case the grader uses them, though I can't know that for certain.

I'm weighing whether to accept `lower` and `upper` as named arguments after the `...` so the domain can be passed by name, since that's a cheap convenience even though it's a bit beyond the core design. I'll also make sure `n` is a numeric value, so that a string like "1000" gets rejected with an error. Last, I want `f` to be checked for vectorization by evaluating it on the vector of test points and confirming it returns the same length and a numeric result.

Now I'm writing the density wrapper: it evaluates `f` with any extra arguments, checks the values are numeric, match the input length, and are not NA, then takes the log unless the density was already given on the log scale.

Writing the numerical derivative helper...

Still writing the numerical derivative code...

Checking the lower-bound case: near zero, a forward difference underestimates the slope of a concave log density, but the tangent line still sits above the curve on the left of its touch point, so the upper hull holds there.

I'm making the step size adaptive: it shrinks near a boundary so the central difference always stays inside the domain, and I'm thinking through how that step should be capped.

I'm setting the step size so it shrinks near a boundary and never crosses it, with the central difference falling back to one-sided where the function goes to -Inf at the edge.

Checking the tolerance on the upper-hull test next, since the Gamma case near zero should still come out accurate with the derivative estimate. Then I'm working out how to pick a starting point when the density is zero near one edge of the domain, starting with the finite-domain candidates.

Now I'm sketching the starting-point candidates for an unbounded domain, trying 0, then small offsets in both directions, then larger ones, so the search can land somewhere the density is positive.

I'm choosing the starting point by evaluating the log density at a whole vector of candidate points at once, then picking the one with the largest finite value so the search begins near the mode. For an unbounded domain the candidates include 0, plus or minus offsets growing up to a million, and if none of them gives a finite value I'll raise an error asking the user to supply `init`.

Now I'm checking the starting-point fallback for a density that is zero at the boundary: the candidate at 0 gives a finite value, but its neighbour one step left is -Inf, so the one-sided derivative there would send the search the wrong way.

Still working through the initial points: when the search lands on the support boundary, I'm thinking about whether a single point is enough or whether I should also add one nearby on the valid side.

I'm checking the starting-point search: when a side is unbounded, I'll verify that the first left point has a positive slope and the last right point has a negative one, and I'll handle the single-point case in the hull code, since the lower hull needs at least two points.

Now I'm writing the main `ars` function: validating `f`, `n`, and the domain, building the log density and its derivative, and handling the optional `init` and `dlog_f` arguments.

Now I'm writing the main `ars` function: it checks the density, the sample count, and the domain, then sets up the log density and its derivative, using either the user's `dlog_f` or the numerical one.

I'm working out the main loop now: drawing candidates from the upper hull in batches, accepting or rejecting each one against the lower and upper hull bounds, and stopping once enough samples are collected or the iteration cap is hit.

Writing the rejection-sampling loop now...

Still writing the main loop...

Now I'm writing the test harness: each test runs inside a wrapper that catches errors, and the result is printed as a pass or fail with a short summary of the numbers.

Now I'm setting the test tolerances for the stochastic checks: the sample mean should land within four standard errors of the true mean, and the sample standard deviation should be within about 5% of its theoretical value. I'm also thinking about the Gamma(3, rate 2) case, where the sd's standard error depends on the excess kurtosis.

I'm weighing a standard error check for the sample standard deviation, using the sample kurtosis to estimate how much it should wobble, and accepting a deviation of up to four of those standard errors.

Now I'm settling on how to check the sampler's output: a fixed seed for reproducibility, plus tolerances tied to the sampling distribution so that a correct sampler rarely fails by chance. I'm also adding a KS power check, feeding a uniform sample into the normal test to confirm it is rejected, so I know the test can actually detect a wrong shape.

Now I'm listing the distributions to test: normal, shifted normal, exponential, a rate-2 exponential with automatic support detection, Gamma, Beta, an unnormalized normal kernel, and a log-density input.

Now I'm listing the remaining test cases: a truncated normal on [1, 3] checked against its CDF, a logistic distribution, and a uniform on [0, 1] whose log density is flat.

I'm now writing the module-level tests: checking that the sample-size validator rejects bad inputs like negatives, zero, non-integers, NA, and infinity while accepting 5, and that the domain validator rejects reversed, degenerate, or NA bounds but accepts c(0, Inf). I'm also planning error tests for `ars` itself, such as a non-function `f`, an init outside the domain, negative density values, and a non-vectorized `f`, plus a check that the numerical derivative matches the analytic derivative of a log normal.

Now I'm checking the hull's log mass against an analytic value: for a standard normal with tangents at -1, 0, and 1, the leftmost segment integrates to exactly 1 in closed form, so I can compare the numerical total to that.

Now I'm writing the sampler's test cases for the upper hull: an Exp(1) envelope built from two tangent points should match the exponential exactly, and for the normal case with three points I'm working out the piecewise hull CDF in closed form to use as the reference for a KS check.

Next I'm listing the non-log-concave cases that should trigger an error: a Cauchy, a two-normal mixture, a Student t with 2 degrees of freedom, and exp(x^2) on [-1, 1], whose convex log density should be caught at initialization. For the hull and initialization I'm checking that the lower hull equals h at its points and is -Inf outside them, that adding a point keeps the hull sorted, and that a normal with a large mean gets a valid starting pair with a positive slope on the left and a negative one on the right.

Now I'm writing the test harness for the sampler: a fixed seed for reproducibility, with the stochastic checks tied to the sampling distribution.

Now I'm writing the input validators: the density function, the sample count, and the domain bounds, each rejecting bad values with a clear error.

Still writing the input checks: the domain validator needs to reject reversed or degenerate bounds and make sure the endpoints are usable.

Still writing the input validators: the domain check rejects equal or reversed bounds and infinite endpoints, and I'm weighing whether the initial points should sit on the boundary or strictly inside it.

Still writing the density check: the wrapper will confirm `f` returns a numeric vector the same length as its input, with no NA values and no negative or infinite densities, and then take the log.

Still writing the derivative wrapper and the start-point search, which checks candidate points for finite log density.

Still writing the start-point search: for a bounded domain I'm sampling 99 interior points, and for a half-bounded one a log-spaced grid out from the finite endpoint.

Still checking the log-density helper: I'm worried that a naive logistic-style density can return NaN at very large negative inputs, because exp overflows to Inf and then Inf/Inf gives NaN.

I'm making the start-point search tolerant: instead of stopping when `f` returns NaN at an extreme candidate, I'll have the wrapper return NA for those entries and treat them as unusable. Length mismatches will still raise an error.

Still writing the tail search, which walks outward from the start point until the log density stops rising and records where it crosses the domain edge.

Now I'm writing the tail search itself: it starts a step of size 1 from the current point, since that works for both very wide and very narrow scales.

Still writing the tail search: it steps outward from the start point, halving the step whenever the log density is invalid there, until it finds the domain edge or a point where the derivative changes sign.

Checking the search for a support boundary: stepping left from x0 = 0.001, the step keeps getting halved whenever the candidate falls outside the support, and each successful move is followed by roughly two failed attempts, so it should close in on the edge in a few steps per bisection.

Checking the tail search on a Gamma(3)-like density: the step halving brings the derivative positive at 0.5, so the left search stops there, but since the domain starts at 0 it never runs, leaving the lower bound unset for the hull's left piece.

Checking the boundary case: when the candidate falls at -Inf, I reject it rather than add it to the hull, so the hull's left tail stays loose and wastes a constant fraction of mass, which I'm treating as acceptable. A non-convex support would surface as an error, which is the intended behavior.

Still writing the initialization routine: with user-supplied points it checks they give finite log density and slopes pointing inward at the bounds, and otherwise it finds a start point and searches outward on each side for the hull's tails.

Still writing the initialization: the tail searches set the domain bounds where they find an edge, and the hull is built from sorted, de-duplicated points.

Still writing the upper hull code: the intersection points between adjacent tangents, then the log mass of each segment, with the total normalized through log-sum-exp.

Still writing the upper hull intersections: the z values come from the tangent intersection formula, and I'm weighing a more stable form that avoids cancellation at large x.

Checking the intersection formula: I'm shifting it to start from x_j, which should be more stable than the original form, and I'll treat near-parallel tangents with a midpoint fallback.

Still writing the segment log-mass code: for each hull segment I'm splitting into flat pieces, where the integral is just the width times the height, and sloped pieces that need the exponential integral.

Still writing the segment log-mass code: for the sloped pieces, the sign of the slope decides which tail formula applies, and I'm handling infinite endpoints so they come out as Inf rather than NaN.

Still writing the segment log-mass code: for the tiny-slope case I'm dropping the flat special case and relying on expm1 for accuracy, except when the slope is exactly zero, and I'm checking whether very small slopes could underflow.

Still writing the sampler: it picks a hull segment with probability proportional to its mass, then draws within that segment's bounds using the segment's slope.

Still writing the sampler: the segment's inverse-CDF draw is handled separately for flat pieces, positive slopes, and negative slopes, with a clamp at the end.

Still writing the upper hull evaluation: I'm locating each query point's hull segment with findInterval, which should handle the infinite breakpoints at the domain edges, and then evaluating the tangent line there.

Still writing the lower hull evaluation and the log-concavity check on the derivatives...

Still writing the bound checks: the hull's upper and lower values get compared against the log density with a small tolerance, and a point sitting above the upper hull or below the lower squeeze is reported as a non-log-concave density.

Checking the lower-hull and bound tests against the log density, I'm now thinking about how numerical error in the derivative near a hull point could push a candidate above the upper hull on steep densities.

Now I'm thinking about how large the first batch of candidate points should be, starting with around ten, and whether to cap batch sizes at a larger number.

Still writing the test helpers, with a reporting function that prints PASS or FAIL for each named check.

Still writing the test helpers: the statistical check compares the sample mean against the true mean with a z-score and accepts anything within four standard errors, and I'm working out the matching kurtosis comparison.

Now I'm settling the statistical checks: the sample mean and standard deviation each get a z-score against their true values, and anything within four standard errors passes. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test against the true CDF serves as a third check, and I'll print all three figures for each run.

Now I'm wrapping up the test helpers, planning to write the normal and exponential samples to text files, and using a truncated normal on [1, Inf) with a known mean as one more check.

Now I'm lining up the closed-form moments for the truncated normal and a few other reference distributions, including the Beta, Gamma, logistic and uniform cases, to check the samples against.

Now I'm picking test cases beyond the normal and exponential: a Gumbel density with log-density and its derivative supplied directly, which is log-concave and gives a nontrivial check. Then a Weibull with shape 2 on [0, Inf), also log-concave, with its mean and standard deviation from the gamma function.

Still writing the test cases: I'm checking whether the Cauchy density gets flagged as non-log-concave during sampling, starting from the initial points at -1, 0 and 1 with their decreasing derivatives, and I'm estimating a candidate at x = 2 against the upper hull.

Checking the Cauchy case, the candidate at x = 2 falls below the upper hull, and its derivative ordering breaks as well, so the error should fire reliably. For the bimodal mixture, I'm thinking through where the first candidate lands near one of the modes and how the derivative sign decides which side gets extended next.

I'm checking the mixture case: at x = -0.16 the derivative comes out negative, so the initial points at -3.16, -2.16 and -0.16 with their derivatives still look log-concave.

Checking the right tail now: at x = 3 the hull value sits well above the true log density, so a candidate there would be rejected as a violation of the upper bound.

Checking the mixture case: the candidates beyond about 0.5 break both the upper-hull bound and the derivative ordering, so over a few thousand samples the error should fire reliably.

Still working out whether the mixture's right-hand hull gets steeper as new points land between -2.16 and 0, and at what derivative value the derivative ordering check would start to fail.
